ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X‑linked recessive disorder caused by loss‑of‑function mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to absent dystrophin, membrane fragility and progressive muscle degeneration.

sections.p: DMD presents in early childhood with delayed motor milestones, Gowers’ sign and rising CK levels. It is the most common pediatric muscular dystrophy.
b: X‑linked recessive; almost all patients are male
Progressive loss of ambulation by early teens

sections.p: Dystrophin links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the dystrophin‑glycoprotein complex (DGC) in the sarcolemma, stabilising muscle membranes during contraction.
b: DGC also anchors nNOS, helping regulate blood flow
Absence makes sarcolemma leaky, causing calcium influx and fibre necrosis

sections.p: The DMD gene (chromosome Xp21) is the largest human gene (~2.4 Mb) with 79 exons. Normal transcription produces full‑length dystrophin; mutations disrupt reading frame.
b: Frameshift or nonsense mutations → no functional protein
Large deletions (≈65 %) and duplications (≈10 %) are common

sections.p: Loss of dystrophin leads to repeated membrane tears, chronic inflammation, replacement of muscle by fibrotic and fatty tissue, and eventual cardiac and respiratory failure.
b: Elevated CK (>10× normal) often the first clue
Progressive weakness follows a proximal‑to‑distal pattern

sections.p: Early diagnosis enables multidisciplinary care, steroid therapy, and enrolment in exon‑skipping or gene‑therapy trials, which can slow decline.
b: Pulmonary function tests from age 5; consider non‑invasive ventilation when FVC < 50 %

t.b: Is there muscle breakdown? Very high CK supports DMD; normal CK makes DMD unlikely
What mutation type is present? Detects deletions/duplications; if unavailable, use targeted PCR or refer to a regional genetics lab
Is dystrophin absent? Confirms diagnosis when genetic testing not feasible

sections.p: Focus on inheritance, pathophysiology, key investigations and management principles.
b: Steroids (prednisone, deflazacort) are first‑line to preserve ambulation

whenToSeekHelp: New onset chest pain or palpitations suggesting cardiomyopathy
Sudden weakness after infection (risk of respiratory failure)

faq.a: They have a second normal X chromosome that supplies functional dystrophin; only carriers show mild symptoms.
No cure yet; therapies aim to restore some dystrophin (exon skipping, gene therapy) or slow progression (steroids, cardiac care).
CK rises dramatically after muscle damage; levels >10× normal are typical in early DMD.

exam: Explain how loss of dystrophin leads to muscle fibre necrosis.
List the inheritance pattern and why carrier females are usually asymptomatic.
Describe the first‑line pharmacologic treatment and its rationale.
